Fe-doped chitosan@SiO ₂ hybrid as a sustainable biomacromolecular 
electrode for high-performance supercapacitors
Abdulkadir Levent
a

Keywords:
Fe-doped chitosan composite
Silica hybrid material
Supercapacitor electrode
Hydrothermal synthesis
Electrochemical performance
ABSTRACT
In this study, a novel eco-friendly electrode material was developed by utilizing the renewable biopolymer 
chitosan as the primary framework, reinforced with iron ions and silica nanoparticles (Fe-doped chitosan@SiO ₂ ). 
Chitosan, derived from natural biomass, offers abundant amino and hydroxyl functional groups that facilitate 
strong coordination with iron species and uniform anchoring of silica, leading to a robust porous network with 
enriched electroactive sites. Comprehensive physicochemical analyses, including SEM, TEM, XRD, FTIR, BET, 
and XPS, confirmed the successful incorporation and homogeneous dispersion of Fe and SiO ₂ within the chitosan 
matrix, resulting in a higher surface area and improved electrical conductivity. Electrochemical performance was 
systematically investigated using cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge – discharge, and electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy in different aqueous electrolytes (NaOH, Na ₂ SO ₄ , and H ₂ SO ₄ ). The Fe-doped chito -
san@SiO ₂ electrode exhibited an outstanding specific capacitance of 404 F g
� 1 
at a current density of 0.2 A g
� 1 
in 
acidic medium, significantly surpassing that of pristine chitosan. Moreover, it demonstrated excellent cyclic 
stability, maintaining 87.6 % of its initial capacitance after 5000 charge – discharge cycles. The incorporation of 
Fe notably reduced charge-transfer resistance, as evidenced by EIS, while Ragone plot analysis confirmed a well- 
balanced energy and power density. These findings highlight the promising potential of biomass-derived chitosan 
as a sustainable platform for the design of high-performance pseudocapacitive materials.
1. Introduction
The rapid growth of portable electronics, electric vehicles, and 
renewable energy systems has intensified the search for advanced en -
ergy storage devices that combine high power density, long cycle life, 
and environmental friendliness [ 1 – 3 ]. Supercapacitors have emerged as 
promising candidates to fill this demand due to their excellent charge- 
discharge rates and superior durability compared to batteries. Howev -
er, a critical limitation lies in developing electrode materials that ach -
ieve both high energy and power densities while maintaining stability 
over prolonged cycles [ 4 , 5 ]. Carbon-based materials have dominated 
supercapacitor electrode research owing to their high electrical con -
ductivity, tunable, porosity, and large surface area [ 6 – 12 ]. Nonetheless, 
pristine carbon materials frequently suffer from relatively low capaci -
tance, restricting their practical energy storage capabilities. To address 
this, heteroatom doping and composite formation with metal oxides 
have gained significant attention as strategies to introduce pseudoca -
pacitance, enhance conductivity, and improve electrochemical 
performance [ 8 , 13 – 15 ].
Chitosan (Chit), a biopolymer derived from chitin, is an attractive 
precursor for sustainable electrode materials due to its abundance, 
biodegradability, and rich functional groups ( – NH ₂ and – OH) that allow 
facile chemical modification [ 16 – 18 ]. Recent studies have explored 
chitosan-based composites for supercapacitor electrodes, demonstrating 
improved capacitance through doping and hybridization with conduc -
tive or pseudocapacitive components [ 19 – 24 ]. Notably, activated car -
bon derived from chitosan has demonstrated a wide range of 
electrochemical performance profiles in various electrolyte environ -
ments. For instance, mesoporous carbon obtained from chitosan biomass 
has shown excellent capacitive behavior across acidic, neutral, and 
alkaline electrolytes, delivering specific capacitance values above 260 F 
g
� 1 
and enabling the utilization of a broad 1.8 V potential window in 
neutral systems. Such performance underscores the versatility of 
chitosan-derived electrodes [ 25 ]. Additionally, chitosan-based activated 
carbons have achieved specific capacitances exceeding 300 F g
� 1 
in 
alkaline electrolytes, alongside long-term stability, with over 94 %

complete cycling retention [ 26 ]. Furthermore, advanced doping strate -
gies, such as self-doping of oxygen and nitrogen using activating agents 
like ZnCl ₂ , have facilitated the creation of chitosan-derived carbon 
nanosheets with high surface areas and superior pseudocapacitive per -
formance, reaching nearly 288 F g
� 1 
[ 27 ]. These findings collectively 
highlight the potential of chitosan as a versatile and effective platform 
for the design of next-generation electrode materials. However, further 
improvements in ion diffusion pathways, electronic conductivity, and 
redox-active site density remain critical for achieving practical device- 
level performance. In this context, the development of hybrid compos -
ites incorporating inorganic nanostructures and doped functionalities 
within chitosan-based frameworks represents a promising direction, 
motivating the current investigation. In this context, the integration of 
silica (SiO ₂ ) nanoparticles into chitosan matrices has been reported to 
improve the mechanical strength, porosity, and electrolyte accessibility 
of the electrode material. SiO ₂ contributes to creating a hierarchical 
porous structure, facilitating ion transport and increasing the active 
surface area available for charge storage. Such composites enable a 
better balance between electrical conductivity and ionic diffusion, 
essential for high-rate supercapacitor performance.
While there is growing interest in chitosan-derived activated carbon 
and its hybrids, direct applications of chitosan – SiO ₂ composites in 
supercapacitor electrodes remain virtually unexplored. In contrast, 
numerous studies have illustrated the beneficial role of silica in 
enhancing the textural and electrochemical features of activated carbon. 
For example, when rice husk-derived carbon is activated without 
removing silica, potassium hydroxide (KOH) tends to react with the 
silica, forming silicates that restrict mesopore development. Despite this 
limitation, the resulting carbon still achieves a remarkable surface area 
of over 3200 m
2
/g and capacitances above 300 F g
� 1
, albeit with 
diminished rate capability [ 28 ]. Similarly, in another study, the surface 
of activated carbon obtained from olive stones was modified by a silica 
coating, resulting in a significant improvement in mesoporosity and 
specific capacitance, increasing from 11 F g
� 1 
(bare AC) to 141 F g
� 1 
(silica-coated AC) and enabling a wider operational voltage window 
[ 29 ]. Other reports have demonstrated that pretreating silica-rich 
biomass with alkaline solutions enhances mesoporous development, 
which translates into improved charge storage performance and long- 
term cycling stability. Moreover, silica-assisted synthesis routes have 
enabled the fabrication of hierarchically porous carbon nanostructures 
with tunable morphology and pore distribution, resulting in gravimetric 
capacitance values surpassing 300 F g
� 1 
and cycle life retention above 
90 % after 10,000 cycles [ 30 ]. Despite these advances, the combination 
of chitosan and silica in a composite material specifically designed for 
electrochemical energy storage has not yet been systematically investi -
gated. While both components independently contribute favorable 
properties — such as nitrogen doping from chitosan and structural con -
trol from silica — their synergistic potential in a single hybrid structure 
remains an open question in supercapacitor research. Moreover, doping 
chitosan-based composites with transition metal ions such as iron (Fe) 
introduces additional redox-active sites that can significantly enhance 
pseudocapacitive behavior. Fe doping not only increases the density of 
faradaic reactions but also improves electron transfer pathways within 
the composite, contributing to higher specific capacitance and better 
rate capability.
In recent years, the incorporation of transition metals such as iron 
(Fe) into biomass-derived carbon systems has demonstrated significant 
promise for enhancing the electrochemical performance of super -
capacitor electrodes. Various Fe-based hybrid composites integrating 
chitosan and activated carbon have shown improved specific capaci -
tance, stability, and rate performance due to the synergistic effects be -
tween the constituents. For instance, Fe-loaded activated carbon fiber 
materials have been reported to reach capacitance values exceeding 230 
F g
� 1 
with negligible degradation over thousands of charge-discharge 
cycles, emphasizing their potential in long-term energy storage appli -
cations [ 31 ]. Additionally, three-dimensional aerogels composed of 
Fe ₃ O ₄ , graphene oxide, and chitosan exhibited notable electrochemical 
behavior across different electrolytes, with optimal performance 
observed in neutral environments due to improved ion transport and 
structural stability [ 32 ]. Furthermore, electrophoretic deposition tech -
niques have enabled the development of homogeneous Fe oxide – chito -
san – carbon films with stable cycling performance and decent 
capacitance retention, confirming the viability of these composites for 
practical deployment. Beyond structural integration, the catalytic in -
fluence of Fe during the carbonization process has also been highlighted 
as a key factor in enhancing graphitization and increasing surface area, 
which translates to better electron mobility and more accessible active 
sites. Materials treated under such conditions have achieved capacitance 
values surpassing 300 F g
� 1 
with near-complete coulombic efficiency, 
illustrating the dual contribution of double-layer and faradaic processes 
[ 33 ]. Despite these advancements, a comprehensive investigation into 
Fe-doped chitosan – SiO ₂ hybrid systems remains absent from current 
literature. Therefore, the present study addresses this research gap by 
synthesizing and evaluating a novel Fe-incorporated chitosan@SiO ₂ @ -
CuO composite, aiming to integrate the conductivity and porosity of 
carbon frameworks with the redox activity of Fe and the structural 
benefits of SiO ₂ . This work aims to fill this gap by synthesizing Fe-doped 
Chitosan@SiO ₂ electrodes and thoroughly investigating their energy 
storage capabilities using cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic 
charge/discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy 
(EIS). The electrodes were tested in different electrolytes (NaOH, 
Na ₂ SO ₄ , and H ₂ SO ₄ ) to understand the influence of ionic environments 
on capacitance and charge transfer properties. Advanced structural and 
compositional analyses were employed to elucidate the morphology, 
elemental distribution, and chemical states within the composite. The 
results demonstrated that Fe doping and SiO ₂ incorporation synergisti -
cally enhance the electrical conductivity, surface area, and redox ac -
tivity of the chitosan matrix, leading to superior supercapacitor 
performance with high specific capacitance, excellent cycling stability, 
and favorable power-energy characteristics. The findings highlight Fe- 
doped Chitosan@SiO ₂ as a cost-effective, environmentally benign elec -
trode material with significant potential for next-generation energy 
storage applications, aligning with the broader trend of utilizing 
biomass-derived polymers for sustainable supercapacitors.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Synthesis of Chit@SiO ₂ composite
The Chit@SiO ₂ composite was synthesized through a direct calci -
nation method. Initially, chitosan and silica were mixed in a 1:0.5 mass 
ratio to form a homogeneous blend. This mixture was placed in a 
ceramic crucible and subjected to thermal treatment in a muffle furnace 
at 400 
◦
C for 1 h under atmospheric air conditions. No further purifi -
cation or washing steps were applied following calcination. The result -
ing hybrid product was labeled as Chit@SiO ₂ .
2.2. Preparation of Fe-doped chit@SiO ₂ composite
To prepare the iron-doped version of the composite, a specific 
amount of urea and ferrous sulfate (FeSO ₄ .7H
2
O) was dissolved in 
deionized water to form a precursor solution. The previously prepared 
Chit@SiO ₂ powder was added into this solution and dispersed thor -
oughly under constant stirring. The resulting suspension was treated 
hydrothermally at 150 
◦
C for 4 h. After cooling to room temperature, the 
solid product was collected via filtration, rinsed with deionized water 
multiple times to remove any residuals, and then dried in an oven at 
80 
◦
C for 5 h. The final product was denoted as Fe-doped Chit@SiO ₂ . The

2.3. Electroanalytical tests
In this study, three types of electrode materials were prepared: pure 
chitosan (Chit), chitosan combined with silica (Chit@SiO ₂ ), and silica- 
supported chitosan doped with iron (Fe Doped Chit@SiO ₂ ). To 
enhance electrical conductivity, graphite powder was mixed with the 
active materials, and mineral oil was used as a binder. The composition 
ratio was set as 70 % active material, 10 % graphite, and 20 % mineral 
oil. These components were thoroughly mixed until a uniform paste was 
formed. The resulting paste was then applied onto carbon paste elec -
trode (CPE) substrates and pressed manually to achieve a smooth and 
uniform surface.
Electrochemical measurements were carried out using an AUTOLAB 
PGSTAT 128 N potentiostat/galvanostat. Experiments were performed 
in three different aqueous electrolytes: 1 M NaOH, 1 M Na ₂ SO ₄ , and 1 M 
H ₂ SO ₄ . A platinum wire served as the counter electrode, and a silver/ 
silver chloride electrode (Ag/AgCl, 3 M KCl) was used as the reference 
electrode. The electrochemical properties of the electrodes were inves -
tigated using cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge 
(GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
CV tests were conducted at various scan rates to evaluate capacitive 
behavior, while GCD measurements involved applying constant current 
to analyze charge and discharge times. EIS data were recorded under 
open circuit potential conditions with a 10 mV amplitude over a fre -
quency range from 100 kHz to 0.01 Hz. These analyses provided insights 
into charge transfer resistance, ion diffusion, and overall electrode ki -
netics. Both two-electrode and three-electrode setups were employed 
during the experiments.

2.4. Characterization methods
The synthesized materials were thoroughly characterized using 
multiple analytical techniques to understand their structural and 
chemical properties. Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) 
was employed to identify functional groups and verify the successful 
incorporation of iron and silica within the chitosan matrix. Spectra were 
recorded between 4000 and 400 cm
� 1

was carried out to assess the crystallinity and phase composition of the 
composites. Cu K α radiation was used to scan a 2 θ range of 10
◦
to 80
◦

revealing crystalline phases and structural modifications due to doping. 
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) was utilized to observe the surface 
morphology and microstructure of the electrode materials. SEM images 
provided information on surface texture, particle agglomeration, and 
uniformity of the composite. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) 
offered detailed visualization of the internal nanostructure, including 
particle size and dispersion, as well as lattice fringes associated with iron 
doping. X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) was applied to analyze 
the elemental composition and chemical states of surface atoms, 
particularly focusing on iron and silicon species. Brunauer-Emmett-

The thermal stability of the Fe-doped Chit@SiO ₂ composite was 
evaluated via TGA/DTA analysis, and the results ( Fig. 7 a) indicate that 
Fe-doping enhances the thermal resistance of the chitosan – silica matrix, 
implying the formation of a sturdier hybrid framework. The initial 
weight loss from ~30 to ~120 
◦
C corresponds to desorption of physi -
cally adsorbed and loosely bound water molecules within the composite 
architecture (consistent with moisture-loss as first stage). The second 
weight reduction between ~200 and ~ 350 
◦
C is attributed to the 
thermal decomposition of the chitosan network: cleavage of the polymer 
backbone (glycosidic linkages), deacetylated amino (-NH ₂ ) units, and 
other structural moieties. The third mass-loss stage seen between ~500 
and ~ 800 
◦
C likely corresponds to decomposition of residual carbo -
naceous structure, oxidative loss of remaining organic fragments, and 
restructuring or densification of the inorganic (silica + iron oxide) 
phases into more thermally stable metal-silicate/metal-oxide networks. 
These trends are consistent with earlier literature on chitosan – silica 
hybrids showing that silica incorporation acts as a protective barrier, 
enhances char formation, and shifts decomposition temperatures up -
ward. For example, Ebisike et al. report in a chitosan – silica hybrid 
aerogel that a first weight drop around 60 – 100 
◦
C (water loss) is fol -
lowed by secondary decomposition around 440 
◦
C and above, due to 
chitosan degradation and hydrophobic silane network transformation 
[ 63 ]. Also, in another study of modified chitosan composites, TGA 
revealed that the composite exhibited a higher residual weight (~33 %) 
after pyrolysis (versus ~20 % for neat chitosan) and the decomposition 
onset shifted to ~450 
◦
C, demonstrating enhanced thermal stability due 
to grafting/cross-linking and inclusion of inorganic fillers [ 64 ]. Raman

confirms that the overall graphitic structure remains intact. Such a 
balance between graphitic order and structural disorder is desirable for 
supercapacitor applications because it provides a compromise between 
electrical conductivity and electrochemically active surface area. A 
higher I
D

that Fe-doped Chit@SiO ₂ possesses a favorable structural config -
uration — maintaining good electronic conductivity from the graphitic 
domains while offering more electroactive sites due to Fe-induced de -
fects. Consequently, this structural evolution is expected to enhance the 
electrochemical performance of the Fe-doped composite in super -
capacitor applications.
